Large-scale unsupervised language models learn broad world knowledge and some reasoning skills.
Precise control of language model behavior is difficult due to the completely unsupervised nature of their training.
Existing methods for steering language models collect human labels of the relative quality of model generations and fine-tune the unsupervised model to align with these preferences.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) typically fits a reward model reflecting human preferences and then fine-tunes the language model using reinforcement learning to maximize the estimated reward while avoiding large deviations from the original model.
RLHF is a complex and often unstable procedure.
The paper introduces a new parameterization of the reward model that enables extraction of the corresponding optimal policy in closed form.
Using this parameterization allows solving the standard RLHF problem with only a simple classification loss.
The resulting algorithm is called Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).
DPO is stable, performant, and computationally lightweight.
DPO eliminates the need for sampling from the language model during fine-tuning and reduces the need for significant hyperparameter tuning.
Experiments show that DPO can fine-tune language models to align with human preferences as well as or better than existing methods.
DPO outperforms PPO-based RLHF in controlling the sentiment of model generations.
DPO matches or improves response quality in summarization and single-turn dialogue while being substantially simpler to implement and train.
Large unsupervised language models trained on very large datasets acquire surprising capabilities.
These models are trained on human-generated data that reflect a wide variety of goals, priorities, and skillsets.
Some goals and skillsets present in the training data are undesirable to imitate in model outputs.

For coding tasks, it is desirable for a model to understand common programming mistakes but to be biased toward generating the (potentially rare) high-quality coding ability present in its training data.
A language model should be aware of common misconceptions without endorsing them as true in proportion to their prevalence in human beliefs.
Selecting a model's desired responses and behavior from its broad knowledge and abilities is crucial for building AI systems that are safe, performant, and controllable.
Existing methods typically steer language models to match human preferences using reinforcement learning.
The reinforcement learning-based objective used by existing methods can be optimized exactly with a simple binary cross-entropy objective, which greatly simplifies the preference learning pipeline.
Preference learning is usually performed after an initial stage of large-scale unsupervised pretraining on a large text dataset.
The most straightforward approach to preference learning is supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations of high-quality responses.
The most successful class of methods for instilling desired behaviors is reinforcement learning from human (or AI) feedback (RLHF/RLAIF).

RLHF fits a reward model to a dataset of human preferences and then uses reinforcement learning to optimize a language model policy to produce responses assigned high reward without drifting excessively far from the original model.

The RLHF pipeline is considerably more complex than supervised learning and involves training multiple language models and sampling from the policy in the training loop, which incurs significant computational costs.

The paper introduces Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), an algorithm that directly optimizes a language model to adhere to human preferences without explicit reward modeling or reinforcement learning.
DPO implicitly optimizes the same objective as existing RLHF algorithms, namely reward maximization with a KL-divergence constraint.
DPO is simple to implement and straightforward to train compared to existing RLHF approaches.
The DPO update increases the relative log probability of preferred responses versus dispreferred responses while incorporating a dynamic, per-example importance weight.
The dynamic per-example importance weight in DPO prevents the model degeneration observed when using a naive probability ratio objective.
Like existing methods, DPO relies on a theoretical preference model (for example, the Bradley–Terry model) that measures how well a given reward function aligns with empirical preference data.

Unlike existing methods that train a reward model from the preference model and then train a policy to optimize that learned reward, DPO uses a change of variables to define the preference loss as a function of the policy directly.

Given a dataset of human preferences over model responses, DPO can optimize a policy using a simple binary cross-entropy objective to produce the optimal policy for an implicit reward function fit to the preference data.
The main contribution of the paper is demonstrating DPO as a simple, RL-free algorithm for training language models from preferences.

Empirical results show that DPO is at least as effective as existing methods, including PPO-based RLHF, for learning from preferences on tasks such as sentiment modulation, summarization, and dialogue using language models with up to 6B parameters.
Self-supervised language models of increasing scale can learn to complete some tasks zero-shot or with few-shot prompts.
Fine-tuning on datasets of instructions and human-written completions significantly improves downstream task performance and alignment with user intent.
Instruction-tuning enables large language models to generalize to instructions outside of the instruction-tuning set and generally increases their usability.
Relative human judgments of response quality are often easier to collect than expert demonstrations.
Researchers have fine-tuned large language models with datasets of human preferences to improve proficiency in translation, summarization, story-telling, and instruction-following.
Preference-based fine-tuning methods first train a neural network reward model to be compatible with datasets of human preferences under a preference model such as the Bradley-Terry model.

After training a reward model, practitioners fine-tune a language model to maximize the learned reward using reinforcement learning algorithms such as REINFORCE, proximal policy optimization (PPO), or variants.
A closely related approach uses instruction-following models fine-tuned with human feedback to generate additional synthetic preference data for targeted attributes such as safety or harmlessness.
The synthetic-preference generation approach can rely on weak human supervision in the form of a text rubric for the model's annotations.

The preference-based fine-tuning methods represent a convergence of work on training language models with reinforcement learning for various objectives and work on general methods for learning from human preferences.
Fine-tuning large language models with reinforcement learning remains a major practical challenge.
This work proposes a theoretically justified approach to optimizing relative preferences without using reinforcement learning.
Learning policies from preferences has been studied in both bandit and reinforcement learning settings.
Contextual bandit learning that uses preferences or rankings of actions rather than rewards is known as a contextual dueling bandit (CDB).

In the absence of absolute rewards, theoretical analysis of CDBs replaces the notion of an optimal policy with a von Neumann winner, which is a policy whose expected win rate against any other policy is at least 50%.
In the CDB setting, preference labels are provided online, whereas learning from human preferences typically uses a fixed offline batch of preference-annotated action pairs.
Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) learns from binary preferences generated by an unknown scoring function instead of explicit rewards.
Various PbRL algorithms exist, and many methods first explicitly estimate the latent scoring (reward) function and then optimize that estimate; some methods can also reuse off-policy preference data.
The authors propose a single-stage policy learning approach that directly optimizes a policy to satisfy preferences without first estimating a reward model.
The RLHF pipeline typically includes three phases: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), preference sampling and reward learning, and RL optimization.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) usually begins by fine-tuning a pre-trained language model with supervised learning on high-quality data to obtain a model denoted π^SFT.
In the reward modelling phase the SFT model is prompted with prompts x to produce pairs of answers (y1, y2) sampled from π^SFT(y | x), which are then presented to human labelers.
Human labelers express preferences between answer pairs as y_w ≻ y_l | x, where y_w is the preferred completion and y_l is the dispreferred completion among (y1, y2).

Preferences are assumed to be generated by a latent reward model r*(y, x) that is not directly accessible, and the Bradley-Terry (BT) model is a popular choice for modelling such human preference distributions (with Plackett-Luce models as a compatible generalization for multiple ranked answers).
The Bradley-Terry model defines the probability of preferring y1 over y2 given x as p*(y1 ≻ y2 | x) = exp(r*(x,y1)) / (exp(r*(x,y1)) + exp(r*(x,y2))).
The authors assume access to a static dataset of comparisons D = {x^(i), y_w^(i), y_l^(i)}_{i=1}^N sampled from the true preference distribution p*.
A reward model r_phi(x, y) is parameterized and its parameters are estimated via maximum likelihood from the comparison dataset D.
The negative log-likelihood loss used to train the reward model is L_R(r_phi, D) = -E_{(x,y_w,y_l) ~ D}[ log σ(r_phi(x,y_w) - r_phi(x,y_l)) ], where σ is the logistic function.
In language models, the reward network r_phi(x, y) is often initialized from the supervised fine-tuned (SFT) model π^SFT with an added linear layer that outputs a single scalar reward.
Prior works normalize the learned rewards to have zero mean over the dataset to reduce reward variance.
During RL fine-tuning, the learned reward function r_phi(x, y) is used to provide feedback to the language model policy.
The RL fine-tuning optimization objective is to maximize E_{x ~ D, y ~ π_θ}[ r_phi(x, y) ] minus β times the KL divergence D_KL[π_θ(·|x) || π_ref(·|x)].
The scalar β in the RL objective controls how far the optimized policy π_θ is allowed to deviate from the reference policy π_ref.
The reference policy π_ref in the KL regularization is the initial SFT model π^SFT.
In practice, the policy π_θ is also initialized to the SFT model π^SFT before RL fine-tuning.
The KL constraint in the RL objective prevents the model from deviating too far from the distribution on which the reward model is accurate.
The KL constraint helps maintain generation diversity during fine-tuning.
The KL constraint helps prevent mode collapse to single high-reward answers.
Because language generation is discrete and the RL objective is not differentiable, the objective is typically optimized with reinforcement learning algorithms.
A standard practical approach forms a shaped reward r(x, y) = r_phi(x, y) - β( log π_θ(y|x) - log π_ref(y|x) ) and maximizes it using PPO.

Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) aims to derive a simple policy optimization method that uses preferences directly and avoids an RL training loop by leveraging a specific reward parameterization that yields a closed-form optimal policy.
The optimal solution to the KL-constrained reward-maximization RL objective is π_r(y | x) = (1 / Z(x)) π_ref(y | x) exp((1/β) r(x, y)).
The partition function is Z(x) = Σ_y π_ref(y | x) exp((1/β) r(x, y)).
Estimating the partition function Z(x) is expensive even when using the MLE estimate r_φ of the ground-truth reward r*, which makes the representation hard to use in practice.
Rearranging the optimal-policy expression yields r(x, y) = β log(π_r(y | x) / π_ref(y | x)) + β log Z(x).
The Bradley–Terry preference model depends only on reward differences, p*(y1 ≻ y2 | x) = σ(r*(x, y1) - r*(x, y2)).

Substituting the reparameterization of r* into the Bradley–Terry model cancels the partition function and expresses human preference probability in terms of only the optimal policy π* and the reference policy π_ref.
Under this substitution, p*(y1 ≻ y2 | x) = 1 / (1 + exp(β log(π*(y2 | x) / π_ref(y2 | x)) - β log(π*(y1 | x) / π_ref(y1 | x)))).
A similar derivation can be carried out under more general Plackett–Luce models.

Maximizing the likelihood of human preference data with a parameterized policy π_θ yields the DPO loss L_DPO(π_θ; π_ref) = -E_{(x,y_w,y_l)∼D}[log σ(β log(π_θ(y_w | x)/π_ref(y_w | x)) - β log(π_θ(y_l | x)/π_ref(y_l | x))))].
The method fits an implicit reward using an alternative parameterization whose optimal policy is the policy parameterized by πθ.
The procedure is equivalent to fitting a reparameterized Bradley-Terry model, which gives it theoretical properties such as consistency under suitable assumptions on the preference data distribution.
The paper discusses further theoretical properties of DPO in Section sec:theory.
The gradient of the DPO loss with respect to the parameters θ can be written as -β E_{(x,y_w,y_l)~D}[ σ( r̂θ(x,y_l) - r̂θ(x,y_w) ) ( ∇θ log πθ(y_w|x) - ∇θ log πθ(y_l|x) ) ].
The implicit reward is defined by r̂θ(x,y) = β log(πθ(y|x) / π_ref(y|x)), where πθ is the language model and π_ref is the reference model.
The DPO gradient increases the likelihood of preferred completions y_w and decreases the likelihood of dispreferred completions y_l.

Training examples are weighted by σ(r̂θ(x,y_l) - r̂θ(x,y_w)) scaled by β, which measures how much the implicit reward model incorrectly orders the completions and accounts for the strength of the KL constraint.
Experimental results indicate that removing this weighting coefficient can cause the language model to degenerate.

The DPO pipeline first samples completions y1, y2 ~ π_ref(· | x) for every prompt x and labels them with human preferences to construct the offline preference dataset D = {x^(i), y_w^(i), y_l^(i)}_{i=1}^N.
The DPO pipeline then optimizes the language model π_θ to minimize the loss L_DPO for the given π_ref, dataset D, and temperature parameter β.
In practice, one prefers to reuse publicly available preference datasets rather than generating new samples and gathering human preferences.
Because many preference datasets are sampled using π^SFT, the authors initialize π_ref = π^SFT whenever a supervised fine-tuned reference policy is available.
When π^SFT is not available, the authors initialize π_ref by maximum likelihood on preferred completions, π_ref = argmax_π E_{x,y_w~D}[log π(y_w | x)].
Initializing π_ref by maximum likelihood on preferred completions helps mitigate distribution shift between the unavailable true reference distribution and the π_ref used by DPO.
Further implementation details and hyperparameters for DPO are provided in the paper's appendix.
DPO can bypass explicitly fitting a separate reward model and performing reinforcement learning by using a single maximum likelihood objective.
The DPO optimization objective is equivalent to a Bradley–Terry model with a reward parameterization r*(x,y) = β log(π*_θ(y | x) / π_ref(y | x)).
Optimizing the parametric model π_θ under DPO is equivalent to optimizing a reward model (as in the reward_model equation) under a change of variables.
The authors argue that this reparameterization does not constrain the class of learned reward models and enables exact recovery of the optimal policy.
The theoretical analysis of DPO begins by defining an equivalence relation between reward functions.
Two reward functions r(x, y) and r'(x, y) are defined to be equivalent iff r(x, y) - r'(x, y) = f(x) for some function f of the prefix x.
This equivalence relation partitions the set of reward functions into equivalence classes.
Under the Plackett-Luce preference framework, and in particular the Bradley-Terry model, two reward functions from the same equivalence class induce the same preference distribution.
Two reward functions from the same equivalence class induce the same optimal policy under the constrained reinforcement learning problem.
The Plackett-Luce family exhibits an under-specification issue that requires imposing additional identifiability constraints to obtain guarantees on maximum likelihood estimates of the reward model.

Because all reward functions in an equivalence class yield the same optimal policy, it is sufficient for the final objective to recover any arbitrary reward function from the optimal equivalence class.

Theorem: Under mild assumptions, every reward equivalence class consistent with the Plackett-Luce (and Bradley-Terry) models can be represented by the reparameterization r(x, y) = beta * log(pi(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x)) for some model pi(y|x) and a given reference model pi_ref(y|x).

The projection operator f(r; pi_ref, beta)(x, y) is defined as r(x, y) - beta * log sum_y' [ pi_ref(y'|x) * exp((1/beta) * r(x, y')) ], which normalizes the reward function using the logarithm of a partition function.
The normalization term used by the projection operator depends only on the prefix x, so the projected reward f(r; pi_ref, beta)(x, y) lies in the same equivalence class as r(x, y).

Applying the projection yields f(r; pi_ref, beta)(x, y) = beta * log(pi_r(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x)), where pi_r is the optimal model induced by r, so the projection produces a member of r's equivalence class in the desired reparameterized form without loss of generality.
Theorem 1 can be viewed as specifying exactly which reward function within each equivalence class the DPO reparameterization selects.
The reward function selected by that DPO reparameterization satisfies the constraint sum_y pi_ref(y|x) exp((1/β) r(x,y)) = 1 for each prompt x.
The constraint sum_y pi_ref(y|x) exp((1/β) r(x,y)) = 1 ensures that the induced policy pi(y|x) is a valid probability distribution (probabilities are positive and sum to 1).
Equation (lag_p) is the partition function of the optimal policy induced by the reward function r(x,y).

The key insight of the DPO algorithm is that by imposing certain constraints on the under-constrained Plackett-Luce (and Bradley-Terry) family of preference models, one preserves the class of representable reward models while making the optimal policy analytically tractable for all prompts x.
The presented framework can be used to diagnose instabilities in standard actor-critic algorithms used for RLHF, such as PPO.
The authors follow the RLHF pipeline and focus specifically on the RL fine-tuning step when analyzing these instabilities.
They draw connections between the constrained RL problem in RLHF and the control-as-inference framework.
The analysis assumes a parameterized policy pi_theta(y|x) and minimizes the KL divergence D_KL[pi_theta(y|x) || pi*(y|x)], where pi* is the optimal policy induced by the reward r_phi(y,x).

Minimizing that KL divergence yields an optimization objective that maximizes the expectation under pi_theta of f(r_phi, pi_ref, β) minus β times the log ratio pi_theta(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x), where f(r_phi, pi_ref, β) = r_phi(x,y) - β log sum_y pi_ref(y|x) exp((1/β) r_phi(x,y)).

The objective in this work is the same as the objective optimized in prior works (Ziegler et al. 2020; Stiennon et al. 2022; Bai et al. 2022; Ouyang et al. 2022) when using the DPO-equivalent reward for the reward class r_phi.
The normalization term in f(r_phi, pi_ref, beta) can be interpreted as the soft value function of the reference policy pi_ref.
The normalization term does not affect the optimal solution of the objective.
Without the normalization term, the policy gradient of the objective can have high variance, which can make learning unstable.
One can accommodate the normalization term using a learned value function, but learning that value function can be difficult to optimize.
Prior works have alternatively normalized rewards using a human completion baseline, which is effectively a single-sample Monte Carlo estimate of the normalizing term.
The DPO reparameterization yields a reward function that does not require any baselines.
The experiments evaluate DPO's ability to train policies directly from preferences.

In a controlled text-generation setting, the experiments compare how efficiently DPO trades off maximizing reward and minimizing KL divergence with the reference policy, relative to common preference-learning algorithms such as PPO.
The experiments also evaluate DPO on larger models and more difficult RLHF tasks, including summarization and dialogue.

With almost no hyperparameter tuning, DPO tends to perform as well as or better than strong baselines such as RLHF with PPO and returning the best of N sampled trajectories under a learned reward function.
Additional experimental setup details are provided in the appendix.
The experiments explore three open-ended text generation tasks: controlled sentiment generation, summarization, and single-turn dialogue.
All experiments train policies from a dataset of preferences D = {x^{(i)}, y_w^{(i)}, y_l^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N.
In controlled sentiment generation, x is a prefix of a movie review from the IMDb dataset.
In controlled sentiment generation, the policy must generate y with positive sentiment.
For controlled sentiment generation, preference pairs are generated using a pre-trained sentiment classifier so that p(positive | x, y_w) > p(positive | x, y_l).
For controlled sentiment generation, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is performed by fine-tuning GPT-2-large until convergence on reviews from the IMDb training split.
In summarization, x is a forum post from Reddit and the policy must generate a summary y of the main points in the post.
The summarization experiments use the Reddit TL;DR summarization dataset together with human preferences gathered by prior work.
For summarization, the authors use an SFT model fine-tuned on human-written forum post summaries and apply the TRLX framework for RLHF.
The human preference dataset for summarization was gathered on samples from a different but similarly-trained SFT model.
In single-turn dialogue, x is a human query that can cover diverse topics and the policy must produce an engaging and helpful response y.
The single-turn dialogue experiments use the Anthropic Helpful and Harmless dialogue dataset containing 170k dialogues between a human and an automated assistant.
Each transcript in the Anthropic dataset ends with a pair of responses generated by a large language model along with a human preference label denoting the preferred response.
No pre-trained SFT model was available for the single-turn dialogue setting.
For single-turn dialogue, the authors fine-tune an off-the-shelf language model on only the preferred completions to form the SFT model.

In the controlled sentiment generation setting, algorithms are evaluated by their frontier of achieved reward and KL-divergence from the reference policy because the ground-truth reward function is available.
The ground-truth reward function in the controlled sentiment experiments is a sentiment classifier.
In real-world tasks where the ground-truth reward is unknown, algorithms are evaluated by their win rate against a baseline policy.
GPT-4 is used as a proxy for human evaluation of summary quality in the summarization task and of response helpfulness in the single-turn dialogue task.
For summarization, the baseline policy is the reference summaries in the test set.
For dialogue, the baseline policy is the preferred response in the test dataset.
The authors conducted a human study and found that GPT-4 judgments correlate strongly with human judgments.
Human agreement with GPT-4 was typically similar to or higher than inter-human annotator agreement.
The experiments compare DPO with several existing approaches to training language models to adhere to human preferences.
They evaluate zero-shot prompting with GPT-J for summarization and 2-shot prompting with Pythia-2.8B for dialogue.

They evaluate an SFT model and Preferred-FT, where Preferred-FT is fine-tuned on the chosen completion y_w from either the SFT model (in controlled sentiment and summarization) or a generic LM (in single-turn dialogue).

The Unlikelihood method optimizes the policy to maximize the probability assigned to y_w and minimize the probability assigned to y_l, with an optional coefficient alpha in [0,1] on the unlikelihood term.
They evaluate PPO using a reward function learned from the preference data.
PPO-GT is an oracle variant of PPO that learns from the ground-truth reward function available in the controlled sentiment setting.

For sentiment experiments they use two implementations of PPO-GT: an off-the-shelf version and a modified version that normalizes rewards and further tunes hyperparameters to improve performance, and they apply these modifications when running PPO with learned rewards.

The Best of N baseline samples N responses from the SFT model (or Preferred-FT in dialogue) and returns the highest-scoring response according to a reward function learned from the preference dataset.
Best of N decouples the quality of the reward model from PPO optimization but is computationally impractical for moderate N because it requires sampling N completions for every query at test time.
The KL-constrained reward maximization objective used in typical RLHF algorithms balances exploitation of reward while restricting the policy from deviating far from the reference policy.
When comparing RLHF algorithms, both achieved reward and KL discrepancy must be considered because achieving slightly higher reward with much higher KL is not necessarily desirable.
The experiments report reward-KL frontiers for various algorithms in the sentiment setting.

The authors executed multiple training runs per algorithm with different hyperparameters for policy conservativeness: target KL in {3, 6, 9, 12} for PPO, β in {0.05, 0.1, 1, 5} for DPO (or related methods), and α in {0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1} for unlikelihood, while preferred-FT was varied by random seeds.
The hyperparameter sweep included 22 runs in total.

After each 100 training steps until convergence, each policy was evaluated on a set of test prompts by computing the average reward under the true reward function and the average sequence-level KL (the sum of per-timestep KL divergences) with the reference policy KL(pi || pi_ref).
DPO produces the most efficient reward-KL frontier, achieving the highest reward while still maintaining low KL.
DPO and PPO optimize the same objective, but DPO is notably more efficient than PPO, with DPO's reward/KL tradeoff strictly dominating PPO.
DPO achieves a better reward-KL frontier than PPO even when PPO has access to ground-truth rewards (PPO-GT).
The study evaluates fine-tuning performance of DPO on summarization and single-turn dialogue tasks.
Automatic evaluation metrics such as ROUGE can be poorly correlated with human preferences for summarization.
Prior work found that fine-tuning language models using PPO on human preferences can provide more effective summaries.
The authors evaluate methods by sampling completions on the test split of the TL;DR summarization dataset and computing average win rate against reference completions in the test set.
Completions for all methods were sampled at temperatures varying from 0.0 to 1.0 to compute win rates.
DPO, PPO, and Preferred-FT all fine-tune the same GPT-J SFT model from CarperAI (openai_summarize_tldr_sft).
DPO achieves a win rate of approximately 61% at temperature 0.0.
PPO achieves a win rate of about 57% at its optimal sampling temperature of 0.0.
DPO attains a higher maximum win rate compared to the best-of-N baseline.
The authors did not meaningfully tune DPO's beta hyperparameter, so the reported results may underestimate DPO's potential.
DPO is more robust to sampling temperature than PPO, whose performance can degrade to that of the base GPT-J model at high temperatures.
Preferred-FT does not improve significantly over the SFT model.
In human evaluations, DPO samples at temperature 0.25 were preferred 58% of the time over PPO samples at temperature 0.0.
The experiments evaluate single-turn dialogue on the subset of the Anthropic HH test split that contains one step of human-assistant interaction.
GPT-4 evaluations use the preferred completions on the test set as the reference to compute win rates for different methods.

Because there is no standard supervised fine-tuned model for this task, the authors start from a pre-trained Pythia-2.8B model and use Preferred-FT to train a reference model on the chosen completions so that completions are within the model distribution before training with DPO.
The authors compare DPO against the best of 128 Preferred-FT completions and report that the Best-of-N baseline plateaus at 128 completions for this task.
The comparison set also includes a 2-shot prompted version of the Pythia-2.8B base model, and DPO performs as well or better than that baseline at the best-performing temperatures for each method.

The authors evaluated an RLHF model trained with PPO on the Anthropic HH dataset from a known source but were unable to find a prompt or sampling temperature that outperformed the base Pythia-2.8B model.
Because TL;DR results and the fact that both methods optimize the same reward function suggest similarity, the authors consider Best of 128 to be a rough proxy for PPO-level performance.
Overall, DPO is the only computationally efficient method that improves over the preferred completions in the Anthropic HH dataset.
DPO provides similar or better performance compared to the computationally demanding Best of 128 baseline.
DPO converges to its best performance relatively quickly according to the reported figures.
The PPO and DPO policies from the Reddit TL;DR summarization experiment were evaluated on the CNN/DailyMail test split using sampling temperatures 0 and 0.25.
GPT-4 win rates against the ground-truth CNN/DailyMail summaries were computed using the GPT-4 (C) prompt with the phrase "forum post" replaced by "news article".
On the CNN/DailyMail distribution, the DPO policy outperformed the PPO policy by a significant margin.
This result provides initial evidence that DPO policies can generalize similarly well to PPO policies despite DPO not using the additional unlabeled Reddit TL;DR prompts that PPO uses.
A human study was conducted to verify the reliability of GPT-4's judgments using the TL;DR summarization experiment and two different GPT-4 prompts.
The GPT-4 (S) prompt asks which summary better summarizes the important information in the post.
The GPT-4 (C) prompt asks which summary better summarizes the important information and which summary is more concise.
The GPT-4 (C) prompt was motivated by an observation that GPT-4 prefers longer, more repetitive summaries under the GPT-4 (S) prompt than humans do.

Three comparisons were performed using a highest-performing method (DPO, temp 0.25), a lowest-performing method (PPO, temp 1.0), and a middle-performing method (SFT, temp 0.25), each compared against greedily-sampled PPO.
With both GPT-4 prompts, GPT-4 tended to agree with humans about as often as humans agreed with each other, suggesting GPT-4 is a reasonable proxy for human evaluations.
Due to limited human raters, multiple human judgments were collected only for the DPO and PPO-1 comparisons.
The GPT-4 (C) prompt generally provided win rates more representative of humans and was used for the paper's main results.
Learning from preferences is a powerful, scalable framework for training capable, aligned language models.
The paper introduces Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), a simple training paradigm for training language models from preferences without using reinforcement learning.

DPO identifies a mapping between language model policies and reward functions that enables training a language model to satisfy human preferences directly with a simple cross-entropy loss, without reinforcement learning or loss of generality.
DPO requires virtually no hyperparameter tuning.
With virtually no tuning of hyperparameters, DPO performs similarly or better than existing RLHF algorithms, including those based on PPO.
The authors' initial results suggest that DPO policies can generalize out of distribution similarly to PPO-based models, but they state that more comprehensive study is needed.
The authors propose investigating whether training with self-labeling from the DPO policy can make effective use of unlabeled prompts.

The authors note a slight decrease in performance in a dialogue evaluation that may be an instance of reward over-optimization and recommend further study of reward over-optimization in the direct preference optimization setting.
The experiments in the paper evaluate models up to 6 billion parameters, and the authors identify scaling DPO to models orders of magnitude larger as an important direction for future work.
The authors find that win rates computed by GPT-4 are impacted by the prompt and suggest future work to study how to elicit high-quality judgments from automated systems.
The authors state that DPO has potential applications beyond training language models from human preferences, including training generative models in other modalities.
